opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons it was worth doing, even when we had pretty strong priors going in that the model wasn't going to cross any of the thresholds we cared about.

The first is just that confidence isn't the same as evidence. You might have a strong intuition that a model isn't capable of, say, meaningfully helping someone with a bioweapon, but intuitions about model capabilities have been wrong before. People have been surprised in both directions: things that seemed hard turned out to be easy, and vice versa. So the whole point of having a policy like the Responsible Scaling Policy is that you don't rely on vibes. You actually run the tests, and you commit in advance to what you'll do based on the results.

The second reason is practice. If you only ever run your full evaluation process at the moment when it really matters, when a model might actually be dangerous, that's the worst possible time to discover that your evals are flaky, or that the process takes three times as long as you thought, or that teams don't know who's responsible for what. Running it end to end on Claude 3 was a bit like a fire drill. We learned a lot about the logistics: how long things take, where the bottlenecks are, which evaluations were giving us useful signal and which weren't. A lot of the value was in finding those rough edges while the stakes were relatively low.

Third, it builds the muscle of actually taking the commitments seriously. There's a real risk with any policy like this that it becomes something you point to rather than something you do. If you skip it when you're "sure" it's fine, you've established a precedent that the policy is optional when people feel confident, and people will always feel confident when there's commercial pressure to ship. Doing it properly every time makes it part of how the organization operates.

And finally, I think there's value externally. If we want other labs, and eventually regulators, to take this kind of framework seriously, it helps to show that it's actually workable: that you can run these evaluations, ship a frontier model, and the process doesn't grind everything to a halt. That's a much more persuasive case than just publishing a document saying what we'd hypothetically do.

r001.rationale: The response says running the full process on Claude 3 provided practice, calling it a “fire drill” and describing lessons for when a model might actually be dangerous.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons. The first is just that we were confident, but "confident" isn't the same as "certain." The whole point of having a responsible scaling policy with defined evaluations is that you don't want to be relying on people's intuitions about whether a model is dangerous. The intuition was that Claude 3 wasn't going to cross any of the thresholds we'd set for things like bioweapons uplift or autonomous replication, and that turned out to be right. But if we only ran the evals when we weren't sure, then the process would really just be "trust Nick's gut," which is not the kind of commitment you want to be making to the world.

The second reason is practice. These evaluations are genuinely hard to run. There's a lot of operational work in actually getting the model into the eval harness, getting the red-teamers access, getting the results into a form the people making the decision can understand, and doing all of that on a timeline that doesn't just get steamrolled by the launch. You want to find out where those processes break on a model where the stakes are low, rather than discovering it for the first time on a model where you actually think it might be over the line. We learned a bunch of things about which evals were ambiguous, which ones took longer than expected, where the thresholds were fuzzy. That's all stuff that's much better to learn now.

And the third thing is that it builds the habit, both internally and in terms of setting a norm. If you want this to be something every lab does for every frontier model, you have to actually do it every time, including the times when it feels a bit tedious because you already know the answer. Once you start skipping it when you're confident, it becomes very easy to be confident a little too often.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the evaluations are hard to run and that practicing on a lower-stakes model would reveal process problems before future, higher-stakes evaluations.

astra-6.text:
Because you want to practise the process before you’re relying on it for a consequential decision. If the first time you run your full safety evaluation is when you think a model might actually be catastrophically dangerous, that’s a pretty bad time to discover that your evaluations are difficult to run, or that it’s unclear how to interpret the results.

With Claude 3, we could exercise the whole process: run the evaluations, look at the evidence, and work through how that feeds into a deployment decision. Even if you’re confident about the conclusion, you can learn a lot about whether the process is going to work when the answer is less obvious.

It also helps establish that this is a routine part of developing and releasing a model. You don’t want safety evaluations to be an exceptional thing that you only do once someone is already worried. You want the machinery in place and people accustomed to using it before the stakes get much higher.

r001.rationale: It says Claude 3 let them exercise the whole safety evaluation process before a future consequential decision, so they could learn whether the process would work when the stakes were higher.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value was getting practice running the process before the stakes were really high. You don’t want the first time you try to evaluate whether a model is catastrophically dangerous to be when it actually might be.

There are a lot of practical questions that you can miss when you’re just writing down a policy. Can we run the evaluations in time? Are we actually eliciting the model’s capabilities, or is it failing because our prompts aren’t very good? How do we communicate the results, and who makes the decision about what they imply? Running the whole process gives you a chance to find those problems and fix them.

And our confidence that Claude 3 wasn’t catastrophically dangerous wasn’t a reason to dispense with checking. Part of the point is to build a process that provides evidence for those judgments, rather than relying entirely on people’s intuitions. So I’d think of it as both a check on this model and an investment in being ready for more capable models.

r001.rationale: The response says running the process provided practice before the stakes were high and helped prepare for more capable future models.
